I remembered how things had been during our great civil war in the nineteenth century. A carpenter in the North earned three dollars a day, measured in gold. In the South he earned fifty, paid in Confederate paper money worth a dollar a bushel. A suit of overalls cost three dollars in the North, one day’s pay; in the South it cost seventy-five, or two days’ pay. Other prices followed the same pattern. So Northern wages were actually twice as high as Southern wages, because they bought twice as much.

Yes, I got acquainted with several people in the little village. One thing that especially pleased me was seeing our new coins being used: plenty of milrays, mills, and cents, a fair number of nickels, and some silver, all circulating among the craftsmen and ordinary people. There was even a little gold, though that was at the bank, meaning the goldsmith’s shop. While Marco, son of Marco, was bargaining with a shopkeeper over a quarter-pound of salt, I went into the bank and asked them to change a twenty-dollar gold piece. They did, eventually—after biting it, ringing it against the counter, testing it with acid, and asking where I had got it, who I was, where I came from, where I was going, when I expected to arrive, and perhaps another two hundred questions. When they ran out of things to ask, I carried right on, volunteering all kinds of information. I told them I had a dog named Watch, that my first wife had been a Free Will Baptist and her grandfather a Prohibitionist, and that I had once known a man with two thumbs on each hand and a wart inside his upper lip, who died hoping for a glorious resurrection. On and on I went, until even that village questioner’s appetite began to be satisfied. He also looked a little annoyed. But he was obliged to respect a man with my financial resources, so he kept his remarks to himself. I noticed him taking it out on his assistants instead, which was perfectly natural. Yes, they changed my twenty, though I thought it put some strain on the bank. That was only to be expected. It was like walking into some tiny nineteenth-century village shop and suddenly asking its owner to change a two-thousand-dollar bill. He might manage it, but he would also wonder how a small farmer came to have that much money in his pocket. The goldsmith was probably wondering the same thing, because he followed me to the door and stood watching me leave with awed admiration.

“I regard it as one of the finest accomplishments of a cultivated society.”

“Certainly, sir. It also has the advantage of being fashionable among the world’s less cultivated societies: any savage can dance.”

Sir William merely smiled. “Your friend dances beautifully,” he went on after a pause, noticing Bingley approaching the group. “And I have no doubt you are an expert yourself, Mr. Darcy.”

“I believe you saw me dance at Meryton, sir.”

“Yes, indeed, and I enjoyed watching you very much. Do you often dance at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Don’t you think it would show a suitable respect for the occasion?”

“It is a sign of respect I avoid offering anywhere, whenever possible.”

“I assume you have a house in London?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once considered settling in London myself, as I enjoy the best society. But I wasn’t entirely sure the London air would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, expecting a reply, but his companion felt no inclination to give one. At that moment Elizabeth was moving toward them, and an idea struck him for what he considered a particularly gallant gesture. He called to her:

“My dear Miss Eliza, why aren’t you dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must let me introduce this young lady as a most desirable partner. Surely you cannot refuse to dance when such beauty stands before you.” Taking her hand, he was about to place it in Mr. Darcy’s. Darcy, though greatly surprised, was quite willing to accept it, but she immediately pulled back and addressed Sir William with some agitation:

“Really, sir, I have no intention of dancing. Please don’t imagine I came this way to beg for a partner.”

With solemn courtesy, Mr. Darcy asked her to honour him with a dance, but she refused. Elizabeth was determined, and Sir William’s efforts to persuade her did nothing to change her mind.

“You dance so well, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the pleasure of watching you. And although this gentleman generally dislikes dancing, I’m sure he would not object to obliging us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is entirely polite,” Elizabeth said, smiling.

“He certainly is. But considering what is being offered, my dear Miss Eliza, we can hardly be surprised at his willingness. Who could object to a partner like you?”

Elizabeth gave a teasing look and turned away. Her refusal had not lowered her in the gentleman’s opinion. He was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley addressed him.

Saturday nights in our village carried a delightful feeling of putting things in order and taking a peaceful breath before starting life again. It encouraged Joe to risk staying out half an hour later on Saturdays than on other nights. When the half-hour and the rum and water were both finished, he stood to leave and took my hand.

“Wait just a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the stranger. “I think there’s a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and if there is, the boy can have it.”

He picked it out of a handful of small coins, wrapped it in some crumpled paper, and handed it to me. “For you!” he said. “Remember! It’s yours.”

I thanked him, staring with complete disregard for good manners and clinging to Joe. He said good night to Joe and to Mr. Wopsle, who left with us. For me he had only a look from his aiming eye—no, not a look, because he closed it, though an eye can achieve wonders by disappearing.

Had I felt like talking on the journey home, I would have had to provide all the conversation. Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe walked home with his mouth wide open, trying to wash away the rum with as much fresh air as possible. But I was almost stunned by this reappearance of my old wrongdoing and my old acquaintance, and could think of nothing else.

When we came into the kitchen, my sister was not in a particularly bad mood. Encouraged by this unusual event, Joe told her about the shiny shilling. “A counterfeit, I’ll bet,” Mrs. Joe said triumphantly, “or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let me see.”

I unwrapped it, and it turned out to be genuine. “But what’s this?” Mrs. Joe cried, dropping the shilling and snatching up the paper. “Two one-pound notes?”

Indeed they were: two thick, sweaty pound notes that looked as if they had enjoyed the closest acquaintance with every cattle market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat again and ran back to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was away, I sat on my usual stool and gazed blankly at my sister, feeling fairly certain the man would no longer be there.

Before long Joe returned. The man had gone, he said, but he had left a message at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes.
